title: TinyViT integration and accelerator results — November 25, 2026
jerry:
Matmul throughput at 80 MHz

The clock is now 80 MHz. A new single-matmul sweep (tk/tm/tn 16–128, bias off and on) shows much higher end-to-end throughput than the Nov 16 run:
- 128×128×128: 19.40 GOP/s end-to-end, up from 9.71 GOP/s. Compute alone: 30.84 GOP/s, up from 28.78 GOP/s.
- Input DMA for a 32 KB transfer: 661 MB/s, up from 129 MB/s.

Where the gain came from
The gain comes mainly from debugging the system, not from the clock change:
- Removed unused on-chip RAM. It forced the interconnect to break DMA bursts into smaller pieces.
- Removed a stale AXI merger that tied signals off. A repo found online presented it as a speed-up, but here it slowed transfers down.

Why bandwidth rises with transfer size
- Every transfer pays a fixed overhead: register writes to set it up, polling for completion, and similar control steps. This cost is about the same whether the transfer is 512 bytes or 32 KB.
- Small transfers spend most of their time on that overhead; large transfers spread it over many more bytes. Measured input bandwidth rises from 74 MB/s at 512 B to 661 MB/s at 32 KB, and output bandwidth from 67 MB/s at 256 B to about 550 MB/s at 16 KB.

Full table: [Matmul throughput by tile size (80 MHz)](#/files/matmul-tile-sweep-80mhz) on ECE496 Files & Data.
stephanie: TinyViT-5M at 90 MHz: 706.09 ms mean per warmed inference, versus 1,192.68 ms on original FP32 CPU and 1,028.36 ms on mixed W8A8 CPU (1.689× and 1.456× faster). On the same 200 labeled images, top-1 results were 153/200, 155/200, and 154/200, respectively. The FPGA handles 40 static-weight GEMMs in 454 jobs per image, including eight resident FC1→GELU→FC2 pairs; dynamic attention remains on the HPS. The fitted design uses 24,435/32,070 ALMs, 35/87 DSPs, and 304/397 M10Ks. Timing uses matched 224×224 batch-one inputs with two Cortex-A9 threads; detailed placement, profiling, and the overview figure are in ECE496 Files & Data. [Full timing table and overview](#/files/tinyvit-5m-90mhz-timing-2026-11-26).
tiffany:
Completed the hybrid CPU–FPGA TinyViT-5M live classification demo on the DE1-SoC. The board’s ARM HPS captures the USB camera feed, preprocesses each frame, and runs a persistent MNN session. The 90 MHz DMC1 FPGA executes selected model operations and the HPS returns ImageNet labels to the terminal and browser preview. Watch the [CPU FP32 v2 demo](#/files/tiffany-tinyvit-5m-cpu-fp32-v2) or the [DMC1 FPGA offload v2 demo](#/files/tiffany-tinyvit-5m-fpga-dmc1-v2) in Files & Data.

Measured mean latency on the same 640 × 480 MJPEG feed with two HPS threads and 20 timed frames per mode. Each line gives MNN inference / JPEG receipt to logits.
• Original FP32 CPU — 1,264.9 ms / 1,435.7 ms
• Mixed CPU — 1,190.7 ms / 1,367.2 ms
• DMC1 FPGA offload — 832.0 ms / 1,003.8 ms
DMC1 achieved 1.52× MNN inference speedup and 1.43× JPEG-to-logits speedup versus FP32 CPU. JPEG decoding, preprocessing, and runner communication added about 170–177 ms per frame across the three modes. The JPEG-to-logits timer starts at complete JPEG receipt and ends at returned logits. Sensor exposure, camera buffering, and display are outside that window. See the [TinyViT-5M board latency measurements](https://github.com/YilingZha233/ViT_fpga_accel/blob/main/evidence/5m/board-measurements.md).

Image preprocessing on the HPS
1. Capture an MJPEG frame through Linux V4L2 and decode the JPEG to RGB.
2. Bicubic-resize the shorter edge to 256 pixels while preserving the aspect ratio, then take a 224 × 224 center crop.
3. Divide RGB values by 255. Subtract the ImageNet channel means (0.485, 0.456, 0.406) and divide by the channel standard deviations (0.229, 0.224, 0.225).
4. Pack the normalized image as a 1 × 3 × 224 × 224 FP32 NCHW tensor for MNN.

Compared FP32 prediction accuracy on the HPS using the same 200 labeled Imagenette validation images, with 20 images per class. TinyViT-5M scored 158/200 top-1 (79.0%) and 195/200 top-5 (97.5%). TinyViT-21M scored 167/200 top-1 (83.5%) and 199/200 top-5 (99.5%), gains of 4.5 and 2.0 percentage points. See the [TinyViT-5M vs. 21M accuracy methodology](https://github.com/YilingZha233/ViT_fpga_accel/blob/main/README.md#hps-accuracy-comparison-on-200-images).

Integrated the second accelerated MNN build with the USB camera and recorded a follow-up demo. The reported MNN inference speedup for that build was 1.67×. The linked DMC1 v2 clip accompanies the earlier comparison. Timing logs and the recording link for the 1.67× build are pending.

Next steps
• Repeat all three modes with the second build under the same camera settings and publish per-frame CSVs, mean and p95 latency, and the follow-up recording.
• Evaluate the accelerated TinyViT-5M build on the same labeled images to measure its accuracy against the FP32 baseline.
winnie:
Softmax

- Reduced RTL cycles 1536 → 1092 → 654 → 606 → 318 → 228. A 4-stage exact divider pipeline reduced 606 → 318 cycles; packed output reads reduced 318 → 228. ModelSim counts accepted start through the last Avalon result: 228 cycles / 3.04 µs at 75 MHz.
- Board measured 5.088 µs per 49-score row, versus HPS INT8 5.404 µs and FP32 12.715 µs (5.8% lower latency vs INT8). Median of five 96-row trial averages; range 5.085–5.096 µs. Timer includes launch, polling and packed readback with NEON-enabled 4 × 16-byte reads; input staging, matmul and optional GELU are excluded.
- Standalone core: 432 ALMs, 328 registers, 1 M10K / 8192 bits, 0 DSPs; packed readback logic excluded. Full SoC: 26866 ALMs, 377 M10Ks, 2 DSPs. All four Quartus timing corners passed at 75 MHz; worst setup / hold slack +2.732 / +0.118 ns.
- Fabric matched all 23520 board-tested HPS INT8 bytes; RTL matched 691488 saved HPS bytes. Relative RMSE vs original FP32 scores: 6.56%, or 4.72% when both paths start from the same quantized scores. INT8 replacement matched FP32 top-1 on 3/3 validation images.
- Reads matmul output directly. RTL covers raw/bias-corrected QK, optional GELU and the next P × V matmul. Normal attention bypasses GELU; HPS stages probabilities for P × V. For 4704 rows, measured rates imply 25.42 ms HPS INT8 vs 23.93 ms fabric before separately estimated transfers.
- [Softmax results and methods](https://github.com/j3rryhu/matmul-soc/blob/softmax/softmax/RESULTS.md) — published softmax branch, 167aa92.

LayerNorm

- Reduced RTL cycles 10588 → 6748 → 4636 → 3337 → 472. One shared reciprocal per token retains exact integer correction. Overlapping buffer reads, normalization, scale/bias and writeback reduces output interval from 14 clocks to 1 once the reciprocal is ready. ModelSim counts accepted start through completed in-place writeback: 472 cycles / 6.29 µs at 75 MHz.
- Board measured 6.362 µs per 192-channel token, averaged over 12 batches × 24 tokens (about 152.7 µs/batch). HPS INT8: 40.487 µs with reciprocal estimate and exact correction, or 157.588 µs with wide integer division; FP32: 7.751 µs. Fabric latency is 84.3% lower than exact-corrected INT8 and 17.9% lower than FP32.
- Board timer includes batch launch and polling through in-place writeback. Activations/coefficients are pre-staged; verification readback, staging, matmul and optional GELU are excluded. Single-token RTL and batch-averaged board timing have different boundaries.
- Isolated canvas: 949 ALMs, 1054 registers, 6 M10Ks / 22016 configured bits, 13 DSPs. Full SoC: 26982 ALMs, 378 M10Ks, 15 DSPs. All four timing corners passed at 75 MHz; worst setup / hold slack +1.610 / +0.119 ns.
- Fabric matched all 55296 board-tested HPS INT8 bytes; standalone RTL matched 200296 reference outputs. Validation output relative RMSE: 3.49%; INT8 replacement matched FP32 top-1 on 3/3 validation images.
- Reads matmul output and writes back in place; RTL covers bias with GELU enabled/bypassed. For 784 tokens, measured rates imply 31.74 ms HPS INT8 vs 4.99 ms fabric before separately estimated transfers. Combined with Softmax and earlier transfer estimates: about 60.9 ms HPS vs 30.9 ms fabric for one TinyViT block, not measured full-image inference.
- Both operators were tested in separate bitstreams. CPU baselines use GCC 4.6.3 with -O3 -mcpu=cortex-a9 -mfpu=neon; fastest possible CPU implementations were not established. Top-1 agreement on three images does not establish dataset-wide classification accuracy.
- [LayerNorm results and methods](https://github.com/j3rryhu/matmul-soc/blob/LayerNorm/layernorm/RESULTS.md) — published LayerNorm branch, 4bd286d. Full comparison and detailed measurement methods are in [ECE496 Files & Data](#/files/softmax-layernorm-results-2026-11-25).
